quests.correctSentence: I'd like an apple, please.
quests.contrastSentence: I'd like a apple, please.
quests.ruleExplanation: Countable nouns like 'apple' can take 'a/an' because you can count them individually: an apple, two apples. 'Some' is used differently, mostly with uncountable nouns or plurals.
quests.nativeTip: You can count apples one by one, so this noun works with an article.

quests.correctSentence: I'd like some water, please.
quests.contrastSentence: I'd like a water, please.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Water' is uncountable, so it can't take 'a/an'; instead, we use 'some' for an unspecified quantity: some water, some rice, some advice.
quests.nativeTip: You can't count 'water' as one, two, three separate items.

quests.correctSentence: — Would you like a banana? — No thanks, but I'd like some bread if you have it.
quests.contrastSentence: — Would you like a banana? — No thanks, but I'd like a bread if you have it.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Bread' is treated as uncountable in English, so it takes 'some' rather than 'a/an': some bread, not 'a bread'.
quests.nativeTip: Bread isn't counted piece by piece the way a banana is.

quests.correctSentence: There are some cookies in the jar if you want one.
quests.contrastSentence: There are a cookies in the jar if you want one.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Some' is the natural choice in affirmative statements about an unspecified quantity: there are some cookies. 'Any' would be used instead in questions and negatives.
quests.nativeTip: This is a positive statement, simply saying that cookies exist.

quests.correctSentence: There aren't any cookies left; we ate them all.
quests.contrastSentence: There aren't some cookies left; we ate them all.
quests.ruleExplanation: Negative sentences use 'any' instead of 'some': there aren't any cookies left. 'Some' would sound unnatural paired with a negative verb.
quests.nativeTip: Look at the negative form 'aren't' right before the blank.

quests.correctSentence: — Do you have any questions about the assignment? — No, none at all.
quests.contrastSentence: — Do you have much questions about the assignment? — No, none at all.
quests.ruleExplanation: Ordinary questions use 'any', not 'some': do you have any questions? 'Some' would only be natural here in a special case, like making an offer.
quests.nativeTip: This is a genuine yes/no question, not an offer.

quests.conceptTitle: Some vs Any: Offers and Requests
quests.grammarRule: Some vs Any: Offers and Requests
quests.correctSentence: Would you like some coffee before we start?
quests.contrastSentence: Would you like any coffee before we start?
quests.ruleExplanation: When making offers, 'some' is used even in questions: Would you like some coffee? This is a special exception to the usual 'any in questions' rule.
quests.nativeTip: This question is really an offer, not a request for information.

quests.conceptTitle: Some vs Any: Offers and Requests
quests.grammarRule: Some vs Any: Offers and Requests
quests.correctSentence: Can I have some sugar for my tea, please?
quests.contrastSentence: Can I have much sugar for my tea, please?
quests.ruleExplanation: Polite requests, like offers, use 'some' even though the sentence is a question: Can I have some sugar? This matches the pattern from asking 'Would you like some coffee?'
quests.nativeTip: This is a polite request, similar to the offer in Question 1.

quests.correctSentence: — Is there any milk in the fridge? — Yes, plenty.
quests.contrastSentence: — Is there much milk in the fridge? — Yes, plenty.
quests.ruleExplanation: Unlike offers, this question genuinely asks whether milk exists, so it follows the normal rule and uses 'any': Is there any milk?
quests.nativeTip: This is a real question asking for information, not an offer to give something.

quests.correctSentence: How much time do we have before the meeting starts?
quests.contrastSentence: How many time do we have before the meeting starts?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Time' is uncountable, so questions about its quantity use 'much': how much time. 'Many' is reserved for countable nouns, like people or minutes counted individually.
quests.nativeTip: Can you count 'time' as one, two, three separate units?

quests.correctSentence: How many people are coming to the party?
quests.contrastSentence: How much people are coming to the party?
quests.ruleExplanation: Countable nouns take 'many' in questions about quantity: how many people. This contrasts directly with 'how much time' from the last question.
quests.nativeTip: 'People' can be counted one by one: one person, two people, three people.

quests.correctSentence: — Do you have much money on you? — Not much, sorry.
quests.contrastSentence: — Do you have many money on you? — Not much, sorry.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Money' is treated as uncountable in English, so it pairs with 'much' in questions: do you have much money? Even the reply 'not much' confirms this pattern.
quests.nativeTip: 'Money' isn't counted as separate units the way coins or bills are.

quests.correctSentence: I don't have much time to explain right now — can we talk later?
quests.contrastSentence: I don't have many time to explain right now — can we talk later?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Much' is the natural quantity word for uncountable nouns in negative sentences: I don't have much time. Compare this with the next question, where the same idea appears in a positive sentence instead.
quests.nativeTip: This is a negative sentence about an uncountable noun.

quests.conceptTitle: A Lot Of: Countable and Uncountable Nouns
quests.grammarRule: A Lot Of: Countable and Uncountable Nouns
quests.correctSentence: There are a lot of tourists in the city this summer.
quests.contrastSentence: There are much tourists in the city this summer.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'A lot of' fits naturally in affirmative statements and works for both countable nouns (a lot of tourists) and uncountable ones (a lot of traffic), unlike 'many', which is countable-only.
quests.nativeTip: This phrase works comfortably with both countable and uncountable nouns, unlike 'much' or 'many' alone.

quests.correctSentence: — Did many people show up to the event? — Yes, a lot !
quests.contrastSentence: — Did many people show up to the event? — Yes, many of !
quests.ruleExplanation: When the noun is left out because it's already understood, 'a lot' stands alone without 'of': Yes, a lot! Adding 'of' here would leave the phrase incomplete, since there's no noun following it.
quests.nativeTip: The noun has already been mentioned, so this short answer doesn't repeat it.

quests.correctSentence: I have a few minutes before my train leaves.
quests.contrastSentence: I have few minutes before my train leaves.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'A few' is used for a small quantity of countable nouns: a few minutes, a few friends. 'A little' would be used instead for uncountable nouns.
quests.nativeTip: 'Minutes' can be counted one by one, and this means a small but existing amount.

quests.correctSentence: I have a little time before my train leaves, so let's hurry.
quests.contrastSentence: I have a few time before my train leaves, so let's hurry.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'A little' pairs with uncountable nouns for a small existing amount: a little time. This matches 'a few minutes' from the last question but fits an uncountable noun instead.
quests.nativeTip: 'Time' can't be split into countable units here.

quests.correctSentence: — Do you want some rice? — Just a little , please, I'm not very hungry.
quests.contrastSentence: — Do you want some rice? — Just few , please, I'm not very hungry.
quests.ruleExplanation: Like 'time' or 'water', 'rice' takes 'a little' for a small amount: just a little, please. 'A few' would only work with a countable noun like 'a few grains'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Rice' is treated as one uncountable mass, not individual countable grains here.

quests.conceptTitle: Few vs A Few: Negative Meaning
quests.grammarRule: Few vs A Few: Negative Meaning
quests.correctSentence: She has few friends here; she feels quite lonely.
quests.contrastSentence: She has a few friends here; she feels quite lonely.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Few' (without 'a') carries a negative feeling of 'almost none', matching 'feels lonely'. This is different from 'a few', which sounds more positive.
quests.nativeTip: The second half of the sentence tells you this isn't a happy amount.

quests.conceptTitle: A Few vs Few: Positive Meaning
quests.grammarRule: A Few vs Few: Positive Meaning
quests.correctSentence: She has a few friends here, so she's never bored.
quests.contrastSentence: She has few friends here, so she's never bored.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'A few' suggests a small but sufficient, positive amount, matching 'never bored'. Compare this with the previous question, where 'few' matched a lonelier feeling.
quests.nativeTip: This time, the second half of the sentence sounds positive, not sad.

quests.conceptTitle: Little vs A Little: Negative Meaning
quests.grammarRule: Little vs A Little: Negative Meaning
quests.correctSentence: — How's your soup? — I need to add salt, there's little in it right now.
quests.contrastSentence: — How's your soup? — I need to add salt, there's a little in it right now.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Little' (without 'a') expresses a negative sense of 'almost no salt', which explains the need to add more. 'A little' would instead suggest a small but adequate amount.
quests.nativeTip: The complaint about needing more salt suggests almost none is there.

quests.correctSentence: Every student in the class passed the final exam.
quests.contrastSentence: All student in the class passed the final exam.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Every' fits general statements treating a group as a whole: every student passed. 'Each' would place more emphasis on the students individually.
quests.nativeTip: This is a general statement about the group as a whole, not a focus on individuals one by one.

quests.correctSentence: The teacher handed Each student their certificate, one by one.
quests.contrastSentence: The teacher handed Every student their certificate, one by one.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Each' highlights individuals separately, which fits 'one by one': each student received a certificate personally, rather than the class as a single unit.
quests.nativeTip: 'One by one' signals a focus on individuals, not the group as a whole.

quests.correctSentence: — How often do you check your email? — Every hour, pretty much.
quests.contrastSentence: — How often do you check your email? — Each hour, pretty much.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Every' is the natural choice with time intervals describing routines: every hour, every day. 'Each' would sound unusual in this frequency context.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a repeating routine, not a one-by-one focus.

quests.correctSentence: — Do we need any eggs? — Yes, we're almost out.
quests.contrastSentence: — Do we need many eggs? — Yes, we're almost out.
quests.ruleExplanation: This is an ordinary information question, so it uses 'any', not 'some': do we need any eggs? Offers and requests are the special exception, not this case.
quests.nativeTip: This is a genuine question, not an offer, so recall the standard rule.

quests.correctSentence: — How much butter should I buy? — Just one pack should be fine.
quests.contrastSentence: — How many butter should I buy? — Just one pack should be fine.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Butter' is uncountable, so 'much' fits the question about quantity: how much butter. 'Many' would only work with countable items, like eggs.
quests.nativeTip: Butter is measured in blocks or grams, not counted individually.

quests.correctSentence: — We don't have many vegetables left. — Let's add them to the shopping list.
quests.contrastSentence: — We don't have much vegetables left. — Let's add them to the shopping list.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Vegetables' is countable, so negative statements about quantity use 'many': we don't have many vegetables. This keeps the countable/uncountable distinction consistent throughout the shopping list.
quests.nativeTip: Vegetables are counted one by one, unlike butter in the last question.

quests.correctSentence: This bag is bigger than that one, so I'll take it instead.
quests.contrastSentence: This bag is big than that one, so I'll take it instead.
quests.ruleExplanation: Short, one-syllable adjectives form comparatives by adding '-er': big → bigger. 'More big' isn't correct English, since 'more' is reserved for longer adjectives.
quests.nativeTip: Short adjectives usually just add an ending to compare two things.

quests.correctSentence: Today is hotter than yesterday — turn on the fan.
quests.contrastSentence: Today is hoter than yesterday — turn on the fan.
quests.ruleExplanation: Like 'stop → stopped', short adjectives ending in a single vowel + consonant double that consonant before '-er': hot → hotter, big → bigger.
quests.nativeTip: This short adjective ends in one vowel and one consonant — that consonant often doubles.

quests.correctSentence: — Do you need much sugar in your coffee? — Just a little , a spoonful is enough.
quests.contrastSentence: — Do you need much sugar in your coffee? — Just few , a spoonful is enough.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since sugar is uncountable and 'a spoonful is enough' sounds like a reasonable, positive amount, 'a little' fits, echoing the pattern practiced back in Level 46.
quests.nativeTip: Sugar in coffee is measured, not counted piece by piece — and a spoonful sounds like enough, not too little.
